result:
On rainy afternoons, the public library feels like a ship that has decided not to sail. Coats drip by the door. Someone turns a page in the next aisle, and the sound carries through the quiet as clearly as a footstep on a wooden deck. Outside, buses send water across the curb; inside, a child is trying to choose between two books about sharks.

I like places where no one expects you to buy anything or explain why you have come. You can enter with a question, leave with a different one, or spend an hour looking at maps of countries you may never visit. The shelves hold practical answers beside wild inventions. A manual for repairing bicycles stands a short walk from a novel about time travel, and both seem to suggest that a stuck person might find a way forward.

Libraries also make patience visible. Books wait years for the right reader. A seed catalog from another decade keeps its pictures of tomatoes. A cookbook opens easily to the page someone used most. None of these things asks for your attention loudly.

By late afternoon, the rain eases. The child takes both shark books to the checkout desk. I return my map to its place and step outside, where the pavement shines under a strip of new sunlight. I have not gone anywhere remarkable. Still, for a little while, I was free to imagine a journey, learn how a chain works, and discover that someone, somewhere, once made a cake with pears and rosemary. That seems like plenty for one afternoon.
